Neonates of the Gulf wobbegong (Orectolobus halei) emerge at a total length of approximately 30 centimeters [Lb = approximately 30 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the constraints of yolk-dependent development in this benthic shark. The corresponding body mass at birth has been recorded at 158 grams [Wwb = 158 grams], representing the fully formed pup after the completion of yolk-sac resorption. This initial weight is notably modest when compared to the massive adult proportions this species attains, and it underscores the substantial energetic investment females must allocate to each pup during gestation. The gestation period itself, encompassing the entirety of embryonic development until parturition, is estimated at approximately 365 days [ab = approximately 365 days] when water temperatures average 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a duration typical of many temperate orectolobid sharks and reflective of the slow, steady metabolic pace imposed by these thermal conditions. The prolonged developmental timeline, coupled with the production of relatively large, well-developed young, indicates a reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring quality and post-partum survival over high fecundity.

As the pups grow and transition from their initial benthic foraging to a broader diet, they undergo a prolonged juvenile phase before reaching sexual maturation. Longitudinal growth studies indicate that the onset of puberty, marked by the first signs of gonadal activity and testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females, occurs when individuals reach a total length of approximately 94 centimeters [Lp = approximately 94 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds to a substantial period of somatic investment, as the young must more than triple their birth length before becoming reproductively viable. The attainment of this pubertal size is a critical life-history milestone, as it signals the shift from exclusive energy allocation toward somatic growth to the initiation of gametogenesis onset and eventual reproductive activity. Compared to other members of the Orectolobidae family, this length at puberty is intermediate, reflecting a moderate pace of sexual maturation consistent with the species' reliance on relatively stable, though seasonally variable, temperate reef ecosystems. Individuals below this size exist exclusively as immature pre-reproductive juveniles.

Female Gulf wobbegongs produce approximately one pup per litter each year, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of about 0.21 offspring per year [Ri = about 0.21 offspring per year] at a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. The maximum recorded total length for this species, representing the ultimate size attained by large, presumably senescent adults, is 256 centimeters [Li = 256 centimeters]. This considerable dimension marks the Gulf wobbegong as one of the larger members of its genus, surpassed only by a few congeners in the Australasian region. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual of this size has been estimated at 127 kilograms [Wwi = 127 kilograms], a figure derived from length-weight regressions and verified against captured large adults. This staggering mass, arising from the conversion of a 30-centimeter, 158-gram neonate, illustrates the extraordinary scope of post-natal growth required to reach the apex of the species' size range. Large, reproductively active adults of this size are dominant predators within their complex reef habitats, occupying a trophic niche that few other elasmobranchs in the same waters can challenge. The achievement of such asymptotic dimensions likely requires many years of consistent feeding and favorable environmental conditions, with the vast majority of individuals never attaining this theoretical maximum size.

Reproductive output in Gulf wobbegong is modest but consistent with the species' life-history strategy. Field observations of gravid females and subsequent litters indicate that females give birth to litters averaging approximately one pup per reproductive event, although litters of up to three pups have been occasionally documented. When considered alongside the estimated gestation period, the typical reproductive frequency observed in wild populations suggests that females produce approximately one litter each year. This low fecundity per event and annual pacing of litters results in a low maximum daily reproductive rate, a common feature among elasmobranchs that invest heavily in each individual offspring. These reproductive parameters are observed under average thermal conditions of 19 °C, the same temperature regime that governs the species' developmental and metabolic rates.

Longevity data for Gulf wobbegong, drawn from mark-recapture studies and the analysis of vertebral growth bands, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] for individuals inhabiting waters with an average temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This considerable longevity, spanning nearly three decades, aligns with the species' slow-paced life history, characterized by late maturity, modest reproductive output, and substantial somatic investment in growth to a large ultimate size. The oldest documented individuals, having reached 256 centimeters in total length and correspondingly massive body masses of 127 kilograms, represent the culmination of this extended life strategy. Over a period of 27 years, a female could theoretically produce a maximum of 26 litters, each consisting of an average of one pup, with a frequency of one litter each year. This exceptionally low lifetime reproductive output underscores the profound vulnerability of the species to any increase in adult mortality, as population turnover is inherently slow.
